facts.one_liner: The Venetian bar where the Bellini and beef carpaccio were born.
facts.why_go: Opened in 1931 by Giuseppe Cipriani near St Mark’s Square, Harry’s Bar is credited with creating the Bellini cocktail and beef carpaccio. Its simple wood-panelled room has hosted everyone from Ernest Hemingway to Orson Welles, and it was declared a national landmark by Italy’s Ministry of Cultural Heritage in 2001.
facts.best_time: October–April for a cosier, less crowded Venice; evenings for the full atmosphere.
facts.how_to_get_there: At Calle Vallaresso 1323, by the San Marco Vallaresso vaporetto stop.
facts.good_to_know: Expect very high prices; a Bellini at the bar is the classic experience. Smart-casual dress.

facts.one_liner: A mahogany Manhattan saloon transplanted to Paris near the Opéra.
facts.why_go: Harry’s New York Bar at 5 Rue Daunou opened in 1911, when jockey Tod Sloan had a Manhattan bar interior dismantled and shipped to Paris. It became an expatriate favourite through both world wars and claims the invention of classic cocktails including the Bloody Mary and the Sidecar. Its address is famously given to English speakers as ‘Sank Roo Doe Noo’.
facts.best_time: Evenings any time of year; the basement piano bar is liveliest late.
facts.how_to_get_there: Between Avenue de l’Opéra and Rue de la Paix, close to Opéra metro station.
facts.good_to_know: Cocktail-origin claims are the bar’s own. Smart-casual dress recommended.

facts.one_liner: A crumbling 18th-century cottage on Bourbon Street, lit by candlelight.

Its brick-between-post walls, patchy plaster and dim candlelit bar make it a contrast to the neon of Bourbon Street, with a piano bar in the evenings.

facts.one_liner: A climbers’ inn beneath the peaks of Glen Coe.
facts.why_go: The Clachaig Inn has welcomed walkers and climbers in Glen Coe for over 300 years, with mountain views from almost every window. Its Boots Bar has a stone floor, real ales, a big malt whisky range and live music. A famous sign by the door—‘No hawkers or Campbells’—recalls the 1692 Massacre of Glencoe.
facts.best_time: May–September for long hill days; winter for snowy peaks and fireside evenings.
facts.how_to_get_there: Off the A82 in Glen Coe, about 30 minutes’ drive south of Fort William; Citylink buses stop on the A82.
facts.good_to_know: Book rooms well ahead in summer. Mountain weather changes quickly—be prepared.

It is reputed to have been frequented by Paul Revere and George Washington. Its low-beamed rooms are a natural stop on the Freedom Trail between the USS Constitution and the Bunker Hill Monument.

facts.good_to_know: Combine with the Bunker Hill Monument and USS Constitution, both nearby.

facts.why_go: The Eagle opened as a coaching inn in 1667 on Bene’t Street. In 1953 Francis Crick announced here that he and James Watson had discovered the ‘secret of life’—the structure of DNA—a moment recorded on a blue plaque. Its RAF Bar has a ceiling covered in graffiti left by World War II airmen.
facts.best_time: Term time for student atmosphere; summer for the galleried courtyard.
facts.how_to_get_there: On Bene’t Street in central Cambridge, about 20 minutes’ walk from Cambridge station.
facts.good_to_know: It gets busy at lunchtime with tour groups. Look up in the RAF Bar.

facts.one_liner: A stone outback hotel on the edge of the Simpson Desert.
facts.why_go: Built in 1884, the sandstone Birdsville Hotel is the social heart of remote Birdsville in far south-west Queensland, near the edge of the Simpson Desert. It is the base for 4WD adventurers on the Birdsville Track and the gateway to the giant red Big Red dune. Every September the Birdsville Races draw thousands of visitors to the town.
facts.best_time: April–September for cooler outback weather; early September for the Birdsville Races.
facts.how_to_get_there: Small planes fly to Birdsville from Brisbane via Charleville or Mount Isa; otherwise it’s a long outback drive.
facts.good_to_know: Book months ahead for race week. Carry spares and extra fuel on outback roads.

facts.why_go: The Pilchard Inn stands on Burgh Island, a tidal island off Bigbury-on-Sea in south Devon, and is said to date back to 1336. At low tide you walk across the sand; at high tide the island’s unique sea tractor carries you over. The island’s Art Deco hotel inspired Agatha Christie, who wrote here.
facts.best_time: Late spring to early autumn; check tide tables and come for sunset.
facts.how_to_get_there: Drive to Bigbury-on-Sea (about 30 minutes from Plymouth), then walk across at low tide or take the sea tractor.
facts.good_to_know: Watch the tide carefully. Opening hours can be restricted for hotel events.

facts.best_time: Weekday afternoons, when there is more chance of a spot inside.
facts.how_to_get_there: In central Bury St Edmunds, about 10 minutes’ walk from the station (trains from Cambridge and Ipswich).
facts.good_to_know: Only a handful of people fit at once—be patient and take turns.

facts.one_liner: A medieval half-timbered longhouse that became the National Trust’s first pub.
facts.why_go: The Fleece Inn in Bretforton began life as a medieval longhouse and became an inn in 1848. In 1977 its owner Lola Taplin bequeathed it to the National Trust, making it the Trust’s first pub. It keeps flagstone floors, inglenook fireplaces, a historic pewter collection and witch marks drawn on the hearth to ward off evil spirits.
facts.best_time: Summer for the orchard garden and events; winter for open fires.
facts.how_to_get_there: In Bretforton village, about 10 minutes’ drive east of Evesham in the Vale of Evesham, near the Cotswolds.
facts.good_to_know: Owned by the National Trust but run as a working pub with rooms.
